newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia braces for nationwide strike.
newsitem.headline: Russia braces for nationwide strike.

text.p: Russia braced for a nationwide day of protest on Thursday which some opposition politicians have warned could turn violent.
Trade union leaders have said that 20 million people will take part in demonstrations across the country against months of delays in payment of their wages or pensions.
Officials in the government, reshuffled on the eve of the protests, have appealed for calm, but say they have no reason to fear the situation will get out of control.
"We have the reserves to maintain public order, both troops and police, and we have taken a number of preventative measures," said Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov.
"We sent warnings to some people about the unacceptabity of provocative actions. But we do not foresee any special difficulties," he told Russian Public Television.
Previous post-communist protest calls have brought few of Russia's long-suffering 150 million-strong population onto the streets and strikes, while common, are often half-hearted.
The unions say seven million workers will strike on Thursday, including miners, teachers and some transport workers.
But officials in key sectors of the economy like the oil industry say they are unlikely to be disrupted. Air traffic controllers have also said they will not take part.
Public transport is, however, set to be disrupted in some towns and traffic in central Moscow will be restricted to allow for a series of marches led by trade unions and communists.

The long-heralded day of protest appears designed to channel frustrations which have built up steadily during the six years of chaotic and crime-ridden economic transition which has opened a huge gulf between rich and poor since it began in 1991.
Unions say workers and pensioners are owed 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) including 10 trillion owed by the state.
They plan to stage marches and picket local administration buildings but union officials have said special security measures would be in place to ensure the actions were peaceful.

Far from opposing the protest, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has been overseeing reforms since December 1992 and who finalised a new cabinet line-up on Wednesday, said he could sympathise with the demonstrators' demands.

"I must say directly that the questions which will be raised on the 27th are in essence at the heart of the nation's lives, they are fair. These problems have been created in the country. That means we must resolve them," he said.

But he urged calm. "I must urge everybody to display wisdom here," he told a news conference on the eve of the strike. "For there are forces who want to...use what might be considered a normal action to rock the situation in the country."
Neither he nor Kulikov said who they had in mind.

The opposition communist party is aiming to lead some protests and a series of opposition politicians, including charismatic general Alexander Lebed, have raised the possiblity that demonstrations could turn nasty.
But all have stressed they do not support violence.

Chernomyrdin said the new cabinet, reshuffled to take the heat out of the strikers' demands for political change, would be able to deal with the non-payments crisis, which is linked to the fact that many businesses and individuals avoid paying tax.

"I am convinced that this line-up of the government will be more effective," he said on Wednesday, putting the finishing touches to a new team whose reformist goals are at odds with those of many Russians, who yearn for the security of communism.
Officials say some extra funds are being paid out to cover wages and pensions. But government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov has said the debts can not all be covered overnight.
